sections.title: Rate of Change and Slope
sections.learning_target: Students will interpret slope as a measure of constant rate of change.
i_cans: I can construct rate-of-change statements from tables, graphs, and situations.
I can apply slope calculations to interpret constant change between quantities.
I can determine whether a slope value is reasonable for a given context.

spiral.intro: Interpret slope as a measure of constant rate of change.
spiral.review: Interpret functions as rules that connect inputs and outputs without relying on formal domain and range language.
spiral.mastery: Recognize constant rate of change in tables, graphs, visual patterns, and situations.

sections.title: Graphing Linear Functions
sections.learning_target: Students will graph linear functions and interpret key features.
i_cans: I can build graphs of linear functions using slope and intercept information.
I can use key features of a line to interpret a relationship.
I can extend a graph to predict outputs within a meaningful range.

spiral.intro: Graph linear functions and interpret key features.
spiral.review: Connect tables, graphs, equations, and contexts that represent the same relationship.
spiral.mastery: Interpret and create graphs on the coordinate plane while connecting points, axes, intercepts, and graphical information to mathematical situations.

sections.title: Writing Linear Equations
sections.learning_target: Students will write linear equations from graphs, tables, and situations.
i_cans: I can formulate linear equations from graphs, tables, and situations.
I can apply slope-intercept structure to connect rate and starting value.
I can design equivalent equations that represent the same linear relationship.

spiral.intro: Write linear equations from graphs, tables, and situations.
spiral.review: Interpret and rewrite algebraic expressions by identifying structure, meaning, and equivalent forms.
spiral.mastery: Represent linear relationships using tables, graphs, equations, and contextual descriptions.

sections.title: Comparing Linear Representations
sections.learning_target: Students will analyze and compare linear relationships using multiple representations.
i_cans: I can construct comparison models for linear relationships shown in different forms.
I can use slope and intercept information to interpret similarities and differences.
I can critique conclusions about linear relationships using evidence from representations.

spiral.intro: Analyze and compare linear relationships using multiple representations.
spiral.review: Recognize common function families from graphs, tables, equations, and contexts.
spiral.mastery: Compare relationships using equations, graphs, tables, visual patterns, and contexts, then justify conclusions.

sections.title: Linear Modeling with Data
sections.learning_target: Students will use linear models to represent and interpret real-world data.
i_cans: I can design linear models that represent patterns in real-world data.
I can predict values using a linear model and interpret the result.
I can assess whether a linear model fits a data situation well enough for the question being asked.

spiral.intro: Use linear models to represent and interpret real-world data.
spiral.review: Write, solve, and interpret equations that model situations.
spiral.mastery: Identify patterns and represent relationships using input-output rules, tables, words, and symbols.

2.1.Graph: PLANNED — slope triangles/line features and graph-based rates are central; WTC, Notes, and every Practice form use a graph.
2.1.Equation: PLANNED — slope calculations and rate statements use symbolic ratios/equations.
2.1.Table: PLANNED — equal-step tables are a primary source of constant rate; every Practice form uses one.
2.1.Context: PLANNED — speed, cost, filling/draining, and temperature rates give slope units meaning.

2.2.Graph: PLANNED — primary representation; students both construct and read linear graphs in every major destination.
2.2.Equation: PLANNED — slope-intercept form drives graph construction and feature interpretation.
2.2.Table: PLANNED — tables generate points and support predictions in every Practice form.
2.2.Context: PLANNED — labeled-axis graphs connect intercept and slope to starting value and rate.

2.3.Graph: PLANNED — equations are reconstructed from visible lines and graph features.
2.3.Table: PLANNED — students find rate and initial value from data tables in every Practice form.
2.3.Context: PLANNED — rates and starting values are translated from named quantities into equations.

2.4.Graph: PLANNED — comparisons include actual graph-vs-equation and graph-vs-graph evidence.
2.4.Equation: PLANNED — slope/intercept features create a common comparison language.
2.4.Table: PLANNED — unlike representations are normalized into rate/starting-value evidence.
2.4.Context: PLANNED — competing plans/rates make comparison conclusions meaningful.

2.5.Graph: PLANNED — scatter plots/lines of fit are central and appear in WTC, Notes, and every Practice form.
2.5.Equation: PLANNED — linear model equations support prediction and interpretation.
2.5.Table: PLANNED — observed/predicted data tables support model construction and fit judgments.
2.5.Context: PLANNED — real-world data, prediction range, and fit limitations are the instructional core.
